outputs.L1:
After Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley

We do not lack people here on the northern coast,  
But they are people one meets, not people one cares for.  
So I bundle my daughters into the car,  
And, with my brother poets, go to visit you, brother.  

Here come your guests: a swarm of strangers and children.  
But the strangers write verses, and the children are daughters like yours.  
We bed down on mattresses and cots, or roll up on the floor.  
Outside, burly old fruit trees stand in mist and rain;  
In every room, bundles sleep like larvae.  

We wake and count our daughters.  
Otherwise, nothing happens.  
You feed them sweet rolls and melon, then drive them all to the zoo.  
Patiently, patiently—ever the father—you answer their questions.  

Later, we eat again, drink, and listen to poems.  
Nothing occurs, though we are aware that you have three daughters  
Who last year had four.  
But even death becomes part of our ease:  
Poems, parenthood, sorrow—all we have learned  
From these of tenderness—hold us together  
In the center of life, entertaining daughters  
By firelight, with cake and songs.  

You, my brother, are a good and violent drinker,  
Good at reciting short-line and long-line poems.  
In time, we will lose all our daughters, you and I;  
We will become temperate, venerable, content to stay in one place,  
Sending our messages over the mountains and waters.
outputs.L2:
After Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley

There is no shortage of people along this northern shore,  
yet they are mostly acquaintances, not beloved companions.  
So I pack my daughters into the automobile  
and, together with my fellow poet-brothers, travel to see you, my brother.

Your visitors arrive:  
a noisy cluster of unfamiliar adults and children.  
But the adults make poems,  
and the children are girls, just as yours are.  

We sleep wherever there is room—  
on mattresses, on cots, curled on the floor.  
Beyond the house, heavy old fruit trees stand in fog and rain.  
Inside, every room holds sleeping bundles, like larvae.

When morning comes, we wake and make sure all our daughters are accounted for.  
Apart from that, very little takes place.  
You give them sweet rolls and melon,  
take them all to the zoo,  
and with endless patience, in the full manner of a father,  
you respond to every question they ask.

Afterward, we eat once more, drink, and listen to poetry.  
Still, nothing much happens,  
though we know you now have three daughters,  
where last year there had been four.

Yet even death is absorbed into our shared comfort.  
Poetry, fatherhood, grief, and everything tenderness has taught us  
bind us together at the heart of living,  
as we amuse our daughters beside the fire  
with cake and singing.

You, my brother, drink strongly and well,  
and you are skilled at speaking poems aloud,  
whether their lines are short or long.  

Someday, you and I will no longer have our daughters with us.  
We will have grown moderate, honored with age,  
and satisfied to remain in one place,  
sending our words across mountains and water.
outputs.L3:
The speaker describes a visit to a fellow poet, bringing along his daughters and joining other poet friends in a search for deeper and more sustaining companionship. This is not merely a social call or a meeting among casual acquaintances; it is an encounter rooted in shared feeling, artistic understanding, and the need for human closeness. The friends are drawn together by poetry, but also by the more ordinary and intimate experiences of family life.

Much of the visit is shaped by simple domestic scenes. Children sleep, eat, ask questions, and move through the day with their usual mixture of curiosity and need. The families go to the zoo, and the poem lingers over these everyday moments rather than presenting the visit as grand or dramatic. The ordinary details become meaningful because they reveal the warmth and trust among the people gathered together.

The poem suggests that poetry and parenthood are closely connected forms of tenderness. The men are poets, but they are also fathers, and their friendship is strengthened by the care they show toward their children and one another. Shared sorrow also plays an important role. The friends understand grief, loss, and vulnerability, and this knowledge deepens their bond. Their companionship is not superficial happiness; it includes pain and remains tender because of it.

Death and loss are present in the poem, but they do not overwhelm it. Instead, they are gently absorbed into the rhythms of friendship, family, and daily life. The awareness of mortality gives the visit greater emotional weight, yet the comfort of being together softens that awareness. In the presence of children, friends, conversation, and shared domestic routines, sorrow becomes something that can be carried rather than something that isolates.

Toward the end, the speaker imagines the future. He sees himself and his friend as older men, their daughters grown and gone, their lives changed by time and distance. Even then, he imagines the friendship enduring. Though they may be separated physically, the connection formed through poetry, fatherhood, tenderness, and grief will remain. The poem ultimately presents friendship as a lasting refuge, one that can hold both the ordinary joys of life and the inevitable knowledge of loss.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores friendship, parenthood, grief, and artistic kinship through the seemingly casual occasion of a visit between poets and their daughters on the Northern coast. Its setting is intimate and ordinary: adults gather, children need care, food and drink are shared, poems are heard, and conversation moves between the practical demands of family life and the deeper pressures of memory, loss, and mortality. Rather than presenting art as separate from daily existence, the poem shows poetry arising from within domestic and communal life. The poets are not isolated figures removed from the world; they are parents, friends, listeners, and mourners.

At the center of the poem is a tenderness built out of small gestures. Feeding children, drinking together, listening to one another’s poems, and making space for grief become acts of connection. These ordinary moments carry emotional weight because they acknowledge both the fragility and the persistence of human bonds. Parenthood links the adults to the future, while grief reminds them of what has already been lost. Friendship offers a way to endure that tension, allowing the speakers and figures in the poem to remain present with one another despite sorrow and change.

The poem also suggests that artistic kinship is a form of care. To listen to another poet’s work is not merely to appreciate language, but to recognize another life and its burdens. Poetry becomes part of the shared meal, the shared room, the shared coastline: one more way people keep faith with each other. The Northern coast, with its sense of exposure and distance, reinforces the poem’s awareness of mortality, yet it also provides a place where companionship can briefly shelter those who gather there.

Ultimately, the poem finds meaning not in grand declarations, but in the sustaining tenderness of shared life. It honors the ways people hold one another together through attention, hospitality, memory, and art. Amid the inevitability of loss and the changes brought by time, the poem affirms that human connection—especially the connection formed through friendship, family, and poetry—can offer comfort without denying grief. Its vision is quiet but deeply humane: love survives in the ordinary acts by which people continue to care for one another.
outputs.L5:
Robert Creeley was an influential American poet whose work helped shape the direction of postwar poetry. Often associated with the Black Mountain poets, Creeley became known for his spare, careful, and emotionally direct style. His poems frequently use short lines, pauses, and ordinary speech to explore relationships, memory, uncertainty, and the difficulty of saying exactly what one means.

The word “Northern” can be connected to Creeley in several ways. Although he was born in Arlington, Massachusetts, his life and work often carried a sense of northern restraint and clarity: a landscape of distance, silence, and reflection. Later, he spent many years in Buffalo, New York, teaching at the State University of New York at Buffalo, where he became an important figure in the literary community. Buffalo’s northern climate and borderland atmosphere suited the quiet intensity of his poetry, which often feels both intimate and stark.

Creeley’s writing does not rely on grand statements. Instead, it focuses on the movement of thought and feeling as they happen. His famous line, “Form is never more than an extension of content,” reflects his belief that a poem’s shape should grow naturally from what it is trying to say. In this way, Robert Creeley’s poetry remains distinctive: northern in its cool precision, human in its vulnerability, and lasting in its influence on modern American literature.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Donald Hall, modeled after Po Chü-i, dedicated to Robert Creeley, about visiting a fellow poet with daughters, friendship, grief, drinking, and domestic tenderness.
counterfactuals.output:
**Visiting Creeley**

I came to your house in the rain,  
late afternoon, the road shining  
like the back of a black horse.

Your daughters ran in and out  
of the kitchen, carrying spoons,  
a doll without one shoe, news  
of the dog, news of the moon.

You poured whiskey into thick glasses.  
We drank slowly, as if the dead  
might be offended by haste.

Outside, the maples shook themselves.  
Inside, the small lamps gathered  
their yellow courage around us.

We spoke of poems, which is to say  
we spoke of hunger, and failure,  
and the friend who had gone under  
the hill before winter.

Your youngest climbed into your lap  
and slept there, her mouth open,  
one hand closed on your shirt.

How helpless we are, I thought,  
and how exact: the bottle, the rain,  
the child’s breath warming your wrist.

Long ago Po Chü-i wrote  
to a friend across mountains,  
complaining of age, of snow,  
of the government, of loneliness.

Tonight there were no mountains—  
only wet fields, the darkening road,  
and two poets drinking  
while the daughters set the table.

Grief sat with us, politely,  
accepting what was offered.  
It did not speak much.

When I left, you stood in the doorway,  
bareheaded in the rain,  
one hand raised.

Behind you the house shone  
with dishes, voices, towels, beds—  
all the tender machinery  
that keeps us from disappearing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem titled “after Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley” set on the northern coast, where poets and their children visit a friend after a family loss.
counterfactuals.output:
# after Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley

On the northern coast  
the day had no edge,  
only gray water  
folding itself over and over  
like a letter no one could finish.

We came with the children,  
three poets in a borrowed car,  
sand on the floor mats,  
apples rolling under the seats.  
No one said much.

Your house stood back from the road,  
windows lit before evening,  
the sea wind worrying  
the last brown leaves  
of the garden.

Inside, the kettle clicked.  
A cup was set down.  
Another.  
The children, shy at first,  
found the old dog,  
then the wooden blocks,  
then the stairs.

They made a small thunder  
above our heads.

You smiled at that—  
not because grief had lifted,  
but because sound  
still entered the house  
and asked for room.

We had brought bread,  
a jar of honey,  
one foolish orange  
from far south of here,  
its skin bright as a claim.

What could we say?  
The dead had already gone  
where language goes  
when it cannot be followed.

So we spoke of weather,  
of the ferry schedule,  
of a boat dragged loose  
in last week’s gale,  
of poems no one had finished,  
of how the gulls this year  
seemed larger, or hungrier.

Outside, the tide withdrew  
with the old patience  
of someone accustomed  
to leaving things behind.

The children ran down  
to the stony beach,  
their coats open,  
their voices blown thin  
and shining.

We watched them from the window.  
For a while  
each of us was thinking  
of a different absence.

Friend, I remember  
how you stood there  
holding the warm cup  
in both hands,

as if heat  
were a message  
from this world  
you had not expected  
to receive.

Night came early.  
The headland disappeared.  
One lamp, then another,  
took up its work.

When we left,  
the children were tired  
and salt-haired,  
carrying shells  
they would lose by morning.

You waved from the doorway.  
Behind you, the house  
was lit and ordinary,  
which is sometimes  
the hardest mercy.

All the way back  
along the black road,  
the sea beside us  
kept speaking—

not comfort,  
not answer,

only the long  
unbroken line  
of its being there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary homage poem combining Chinese classical plainness with mid-century American poetry, involving Robert Creeley, daughters, zoo trips, shared meals, poems, sorrow, and brotherhood.
counterfactuals.output:
**After the Zoo**

The morning was clear,  
not bright—  
a cup rinsed and set down.

We took our daughters  
to see the animals.  
The bear turned once  
in his brown coat.  
The cranes stood  
as if remembering water.

Robert walked beside me,  
small steps,  
his words held back  
until they were needed.

The girls ran ahead,  
naming what they loved.  
Tiger. Monkey. Swan.  
Their voices made  
a little bridge  
over the day’s sorrow.

At noon we shared bread,  
apples, tea from a paper cup.  
Nothing was enough.  
Everything was given.

We spoke of poems—  
how they arrive  
like a friend at dusk,  
empty-handed,  
and still you make room.

Clouds gathered  
above the city trees.  
The elephants lifted dust  
and let it fall.

Brother, I said,  
or meant to say.  
He looked away  
toward the children,  
toward the gate,  
toward all we could not keep.

In the plain bowl  
of the afternoon  
there was rice, there was salt,  
there was laughter,  
and under it  
the old river moving.

We went home slowly.  
Each daughter carried  
a small paper animal.

That night I wrote  
four lines,  
crossed out three.

The moon stayed  
where it was.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a Donald Hall-like poem addressed to Robert Creeley: narrative, intimate, about poets gathering with their daughters, sleeping on floors, eating cake by firelight, and reflecting on death and aging.
counterfactuals.output:
**To Robert, After the Reading**

Robert, do you remember  
how the daughters took the beds,  
as daughters should,  
and we, famous in our small rooms,  
lay down on floors  
with coats for pillows?

All day we had been poets—  
answering questions,  
signing books with the slow  
humility of men  
who want to be remembered  
and are ashamed of wanting.

Then night came down  
on the rented house.  
The girls, still young enough  
to laugh without weather in it,  
cut the cake unevenly.  
Someone had baked it  
in a pan blackened at the rim,  
and we ate by firelight,  
crumbs on our knees,  
plates balanced on books  
we had not written.

You sat close to the stove,  
small and bright-eyed,  
your voice catching  
as it always did,  
as if each word  
had to cross a river  
on stones.

Outside, the maples  
were losing themselves.  
Inside, our daughters  
leaned against each other,  
sleepy, beautiful, bored  
by poetry and therefore safe.  
We watched them  
with the old astonishment:  
that life had gone on  
without asking us,  
that it had made these women  
from our lust, our absence,  
our apologies.

Later, when the fire  
collapsed into its red thought,  
we spoke of the dead—  
not solemnly, not yet.  
We named them the way men  
check the locks at night:  
first this one, then that one,  
then another we had loved badly  
or not enough.

Death stood in the room  
politely, warming its hands.

You said something  
I have forgotten  
except for the mercy in it.  
I answered with a story  
that made the daughters laugh  
from the staircase,  
where they had been listening.

Old age was not yet ours,  
but it had begun  
to send its letters:  
the stiff knee, the lost name,  
the friend whose silence  
lengthened into fact.

At dawn, Robert,  
we rose from the floor  
like boys after a shipwreck.  
Our backs hurt.  
Our mouths tasted of sugar  
and smoke.  
The daughters slept on,  
their hair poured over pillows,  
as if the world  
had not already started  
taking everything back.

We stood in the kitchen  
drinking coffee from chipped cups,  
two poets, two fathers,  
grateful for cake,  
for fire,  
for the borrowed house,  
for the brief republic  
of the living.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

after Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley

The rain lets go  
of the eaves  
one drop  
at a time.

No doctrine in it,  
only the roof  
answering weather.

I sit by the lamp  
with tea gone pale,  
thinking how a friend  
is sometimes nearer  
in absence—

a cup set down  
in another province,  
a sleeve brushed  
with snow.

What did we want  
from the world?  
A little room,  
a road returning,  
words plain enough  
to carry hunger  
without complaint.

Tonight the wind  
turns the bamboo  
and the page  
turns with it.

Somewhere  
you are listening  
to the small noise  
a life makes  
when it stops asking  
to be more.

So we write  
less fiercely now,  
not because the fire  
has failed,

but because  
the ash is useful,  
and warm.

At last  
we become old, temperate,  
sending messages  
over mountains and waters.
